I have done the original P90X, and am 2 'phases' into P90X3 (currently in the 'normal' schedule, but most likely will repeat and do the 'mass' schedule). I like the compressed schedule of 30 mins for each workout, and I always (so far) feel challenged, but as I don't live near a gym, it's never really been an option to do traditional free weight/strength training without some significant investment into weights.

I was wondering about the difference you've seen between these 2 programs in terms of overall fitness/muscle/size gains. Also, any suggestions on supplements that worked well if you did P90X, or other augmentation for this workout routine.
Can anyone provide a comparison between P90X3 (or any P90 program really) and traditional strength training (i.e. having done both)?

So, I'm no expert, but I've used P90X, P90X3, and I currently lift in a gym. I like both and I think they fit different goals.

For the way I work, P90X and P90X3 were good for general fitness and cardio, but don't hold a candle to the strength I was able to build in the gym. I got more muscle mass in a month at the gym than I ever did doing P90X, which I attribute to the fact that with P90X the most weight I was ever handling was ~65 lbs doing lawnmowers (discounting bodyweight moves like pull-ups). With P90X3 it's even less. It probably didn't help me that my pull-up bar started pulling my doorframe apart, lol. BUT, my cardio was better when I was doing P90X. 30 minutes of high-intensity movement every day did wonders for my endurance.

What I like about P90X is that you don't have to think about your routine. You just put the disk in and push play. At the gym, you have to have your own routine and you're responsible for sticking to it.

Eventually I'm gonna have to cut (ugh), and when I do, I'll probably go back to my P90X3 DVDs.

Great info. What were your original goals, if you dont mind me asking, size? strength? appearance? general fitness? better health? I don't really want to get larger per se, but I am working toward general better health and endurance and want to lose body fat.

Originally I had an "oh shit" moment about how fat I'd gotten, and I need to lose weight. If I'm 100% honest, I was working out because I felt my body was one more excuse why I was having trouble with women, and I wanted to remove that excuse. That's still there, but has shifted more into a general desire to look better and be overall stronger. I recognize that many people don't, but I actually enjoy lifting. I like fighting against the resistance of the weight. It's weird, but I like impressing myself with my progress. I never thought I'd be able to pull 300 pounds off the ground and now I can. Repeatedly and without injuring myself, even.

I definitely understand not wanting to get bigger; I'm flat tired of having to buy new pants, lol. You can tailor your routine to not add bulk, it's certainly not something that happens by accident.

I think for your goals, P90X is a good system. I think there are better routines out there, but they're a lot more work just to track down; P90X is complete out-of-the-box. Just don't ignore your diet. Diet is my downfall. My gut is beer and cheesburgers and super burritos, because I don't know that life is worth living without them. I want to feel like abs are worth more than delicious, delicious food, but I've just always failed in making it a priority, hahaha.

Food is tough, and to be honest, I have a hard time finding a healthy diet that isn't either a)overall expensive or b)a TON of cooking (which I hate). Do you just buy the right food, do a lot of cooking on your own, or some other secret I've never heard of? I've managed to drop some weight across each iteration of the program, but the diet I maintain while working out falls flat after I'm done because I just don't want to eat another chicken breast/rice/veggie combo plate. I've seen some websites/apps that promise to develop a mealplan for you, but haven't really given them a chance.

Maybe I'm just looking to hand off too much responsibility, lol.
Having a gut instead of abs is just a body fat percentage issue. Cut harder or longer, for that it's a how much you eat issue not a what you eat issue.
Fat comes off in the same order in went on. That's why belly fat is so hard to loose: it's the first fat you put on.
damnit. That is the most annoying part of my body...

The only time I actually lost weight from dieting is when I went Keto. I dropped about 20 pounds in 3 months, but it's really hard to maintain if you eat out at all and I've fallen off the wagon pretty hard.

I highly recommend learing to love to cook. It's significantly cheaper, the food you make is always healthier that what you get at a restaurant, you have much more control over what you put in your body, you get correct-for-you portion sizes without having to pay premium for "double meat", etc. To that end, Good Eats is a fantastic resource. Alton Brown will make you excited and confident about cooking. Start with just a couple meals that you enjoy and learn how to make them to your taste. I've ruined myself on eating steaks at restaurants because I cook them much better for how I like to eat them. I hate paying for omelettes in restaurants because I know firsthand how cheap they are to make (3 eggs and leftovers is not worth $8.95). Yes, you have to plan a little bit, but it's very worth it. And it's impressive to those around you if you're looking to make a good impression on someone.

Ultimately the key is what everyone says: if you want to lose weight, calories in MUST be less than calories out. Now, actually DOING that is the hard part. I'm a fan of finding all the little things you can do rather than trying to make broad, sweeping changes. Don't drink any calories, for one. Liquid calories aren't satisfying to your body and typically have no nutrition associated with them. Be aware of what actually feels satisfying to eat and what's not; for me, keto worked because fats are satisfying. On keto, a typical dinner was a steak with cream pan sauce and a side of steamed broccoli with butter and garlic salt. That's fucking tasty, and I'm full when I'm done eating. When I go to In-and-Out, I just skip the fries and order an extra patty on my burger. 5 minutes after I walk out the door, I don't miss not having the extra carbs. Contrast that with the typical "diet food" of a plain salad (ugh) and low-fat, well, anything (double-ugh), sweet jeebus why punish yourself like that?

I get what you're saying about cooking, and am lucky (currently) to have a wife that loves to cook. I just feel bad asking her to prep a ton of meals just so I can stay on my diet, so yeah, I'll probably have to bite the bullet and just learn to do it well (not sure I will love it, but I am incredibly cheap, so the savings will make it easier).

So let me ask you this, when you go out with friends/family, do you just not get anything? Is it infrequent enough it doesn't impact you?

It's kinda like being vegetarian; there's typically some menu choices that will work for you, though you might have to ask for a substitution. Like I said, I've fallen off the wagon, but I could order burgers without the bun and with a salad instead of fries, with pizza I'd just make sure we got a topping-heavy pizza and then I'd just scrape the cheese and toppings off the top and forgo the crust (which feels a bit wasteful, but they're the ones that insisted on pizza). At diners, I could get an omelette and skip the toast and potatoes. Etc.

Living with someone else certainly complicates any dietary changes. When you figure out how you want to change your diet, I'd talk to your wife about it. Maybe she wants to join you, in which case everything is awesome and easy. Maybe she can work your restrictions into her cooking in a way that has minimal impact, i.e. have the carbs in a side dish that you can just skip. Or maybe it's a knock-down flat-out battle and you have no choice but to separately buy groceries and bake y'own damn cookies.

And I alluded to this above but didn't explicitly state it; diet is like exercise, the best routine is the one you can actually stick with. If the thought of another plain chicken breast with steamed veggies makes you want to stick a fork in your eye, then that's not the right diet for you. It comes down to your goals; are you looking to lose every pound of fat you can as quickly as you can? Then maybe it's worth sacrificing enjoying food and treating it strictly as fuel to maintain your body. I think for the bulk of us, though, getting in shape is about better enjoying life, and sacrificing one thing you enjoy in an attempt to get another isn't how you do that. When I was dieting, I still allowed myself to eat anything that I had a specific craving for. It wasn't off-limits for me to eat, I was just choosing not to eat it then because I knew I didn't actively want it, I was just eating it out of convenience or habit. It's MUCH easier to stick to "I don't eat that" than "I can't eat that"/"I'm not allowed to eat that".

For me it's a general trend toward being healthier. The Keto idea seems very interesting to me as my problem was that I was limiting the fats (probably me just being naive) too much. That eliminated a lot of the food that I really like, like steaks and bacon and cheese. I'm definitely going to be looking into that. I think my real challenge would be sugar, but I think that is something I could handle more easily than fats in general. I appreciate the feedback both for the information/perspective as well as making me realize I have more research to do. The wife actually doesn't complain, but we have a small son and a daughter on the way, so I'm not sure she's going to have the time to maintain her position as chef, and I don't really feel like it's terribly fair, so I'll pick that up in time, but in general we do eat and enjoy the same things so it would be a nice change for her to have me share the cooking, especially if I am the one driving the menu. She's a fan of the sweets, so I'll task her with making sure she eats them before I can find them.
Yeah, it's definitely an ongoing and never-ending process. Just changing habits here and there as you can, discarding bad ones and reinforcing good ones. Good luck with it!
